newsitem.title: USA: States investigating alleged fraud at retailers.
newsitem.headline: States investigating alleged fraud at retailers.

text.p: Some 25 states and federal agencies are investigating allegedly fradulent debt collection activities by Sears, Roebuck and Co. and whether the practice is widespread among retailers, officials said Wednesday.

The attorneys general of 25 states, the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Trade Commission held a telephone conference call late Tuesday to coordinate an investigation into Sears and other retailers, officials said.

A U.S. Bankruptcy Court judge has said that as a matter of company policy, Sears misled many of its once-bankrupt credit card holders into believing they had to repay their debts to the company, even though those debts were nullified by the bankruptcy court.

"Massachusetts and the other states have expressed an interest in determining whether there might be other companies engaging in this conduct," Chris Barry-Smith, an assistant attorney general in Massachusetts, said.
"Consumer complaints are just starting to surface about other companies since the Sears matter was in the press," Barry-Smith said. "We have no idea how common it might be."

The 25 states, including New York, California, Illinois, and Florida, will interview consumers and then, if necessary, assess damages against retailers, said George Weber, head of the consumer protection division with the Massachusetts attorney general's office.
New England department store chain Filene's was hit with a class-action lawsuit late Tuesday filed by two individuals who alleged the retailer engaged in the same practices as Sears.

The suit alleged Filene's failed to file with a bankruptcy court, as required by law, a "reaffirmation agreement" with the individuals to repay their debts even though they had been discharged by a bankruptcy court.
"Filene's derived substantial profits from its undisclosed "reaffirmation agreement" scheme," the suit alleged.
St. Louis-based May Department Stores Co., which owns Filene's, declined to comment on the lawsuit.
On April 16, the U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Boston ordered Sears to stop the practice in Massachusetts, where it affected more than 2,700 customers during a two-year period ending in January.
The U.S. Bankruptcy Court judge indicated she may order Sears to pay punitive damages of $1.36 million, but has so far reserved judgment.

A U.S. District Court judge ordered Sears Monday to halt the allegedly fraudulent activities nationwide. The U.S. Attorney's office in Massachusetts is also seeking civil penalties and restitution for debtors victimised by Sears.
Sears said from 1992 through February 1997, it reached about $400 million nationwide in so-called reaffirmation agreements with card holders who agreed to pay their debts.
The Hoffman Estates, Ill. retailer was conducuting a nationwide audit of those agreements to see which were improperly handled.
The nation's second largest retailer has admitted it engaged in "flawed" legal tactics, and has said it will repay customers who were wronged, which could cost Sears tens of millions of dollars.
